title: T1596.005 — Search Open Technical Databases - Scan Databases
subtitle: Watch a fictional attack called Operation Open Book .
aria: Diagram of Operation Open Book. An attacker queries an internet-scan database about Ridgeline Utilities, reviews service banners of exposed systems, and ranks targets. The SOC sees the same exposure through an external attack surface platform and closes the gaps. The full story is written below the diagram.

nodes.label: Sensitive data
nodes.tip: Sensitive data - What is at risk

steps.title: Search the index by organization
steps.caption: The attacker opens a public scan-database service in a browser and searches for the organization name org:"Ridgeline Utilities" . The service returns a tidy list: internet-facing IP addresses, open ports, and product names. What the SOC sees: nothing. The query never touched Ridgeline
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Review service banners
steps.caption: The attacker reads the stored banners. One Windows host answers on RDP port 3389, open to the whole internet. An old VPN appliance reports its firmware version right in the banner - and that version is years out of date. What the SOC sees: the same banners, if the SOC looks - crawler user agents like Shodan and CensysInspect appear in web logs as expected baseline noise
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Find forgotten systems
steps.caption: A second query lists every service on Ridgeline’s address range. It shows a test FTP server with a default install page - a system nobody remembered. What the SOC sees: an EASM platform diff would have flagged this host as “new” weeks ago - if someone read the report
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Spot default-credential devices
steps.caption: The camera banner reveals the exact model. That model ships with well-known default passwords. This is a flag for the attacker. What the SOC sees: IoT with default credentials is a critical finding - segment or replace it

steps.caption: The attacker ranks targets: the VPN appliance first, because its old firmware has a known flaw; the RDP host second, for password guessing. What the SOC sees: internet-facing remediation should follow the same order - fix by exposure

steps.title: SOC view: change detection
steps.caption: On the defender side, the EASM platform compares this week’s scan with last week’s and flags a new exposure. Crawler user agents remain in the web logs as a steady baseline - useful for correlating what changed. What the SOC sees: the early warning that the attacker already has this data

steps.title: One careful verification probe
steps.caption: The attacker wants to be sure the index is current, so they send a single, quiet probe to the VPN appliance and read the banner directly. One packet. What the SOC sees: almost nothing - a lone connection among thousands. Assume indexed data is enough for attackers; do not wait to catch this probe
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Defenders close the gaps
steps.caption: The SOC responds: the FTP server is closed, the VPN appliance is patched with multi-factor authentication (MFA) enforced, RDP moves behind the VPN, the camera is segmented. A weekly EASM review becomes routine. What the SOC sees: a shorter list in next week’s index - the goal of the whole exercise
